title: Sole Meunière
subtitle: Classic French pan-fried sole in beurre noisette
excerpt: The simplest and most perfect fish dish in French cooking: whole Dover sole dredged in flour, pan-fried in clarified butter until golden, finished with a sauce of beurre noisette, lemon, and parsley. Elegance at its absolute purest.

recipe.sourceNotes: Sole meunière (literally 'miller's wife's sole', referring to the flour coating) is a cornerstone of French classical cooking and one of the most frequently cited examples of la cuisine simple française. The dish was Julia Child's transformative first meal in France, eaten in Rouen in 1948, which she described as the beginning of her love of French food. The technique is minimal: the sole is dusted with seasoned flour, fried skin-on in clarified butter or a butter-oil mixture, then the same pan is used to make a beurre noisette (brown butter) that is deglazed with lemon juice and poured over the fish with chopped parsley. The quality of the fish is everything; Dover sole is the finest choice, but lemon sole or other flat fish produce excellent results.

content.text: The beurre noisette is the crucial final step; it transforms in a matter of seconds from brown butter to burnt butter. Watch it closely: it should be amber and smell of hazelnuts when the lemon juice goes in. Pour it over the fish immediately. The fish takes only a few minutes per side; the flesh should just release from the bone when lifted with a fork.

items.preparation: Dover or lemon sole; 4 large fillets; substitute a whole sole (ask the fishmonger to skin it) if available
60 g for frying; 40 g for the beurre noisette

content.text: Season the flour well. Dredge the sole in the seasoned flour on both sides; shake off the excess. The flour coating should be thin and even.
Heat 60 g butter with the oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat until foaming. Add the sole. Fry for 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden. Remove to warm plates.

Wipe the pan clean. Add the remaining 40 g butter over medium-high heat. Swirl as it melts and foams. When the foam subsides and the butter turns amber and smells nutty, remove from the heat and add the lemon juice; it will sizzle. Add the parsley. Pour immediately over the fish and serve at once.
